title: Już nie, jeszcze nie
title_en: Not any more, not yet, not any
note: C1 Block 9, unit 3. ONE IDEA, STATED AS THE UNIT'S TITLE SLIDE: what a nie does to three words. juz and jeszcze FLIP into their own opposites when a nie lands on the verb, and zaden exists ONLY in a negative sentence. That framing is what lets the spine's two halves sit in one unit without breaking the load-splitting rule - they are not two systems, they are one fact about negative polarity seen on invariable words and then on a declining one. SEVEN NEW STRINGS, ZERO NEW ENDINGS. juz nie and jeszcze nie are pairs of words the learner already owns separately (juz/jeszcze <- b2_conjunctions [133], which taught them in their POSITIVE jobs and fenced both negative senses absolutely). zaden/zadna/zadne/zadnego/zadnej are the one new word, and every ending it takes is owned: the m/f/n nominative is the ten_ta_to shape, and -ego/-ej are b2_adj_gen's own genitive endings, already produced on dobrego/dobrej/nowego/nowej. THIS PAYS b2_double_neg's LOGGED SCOPE CUT IN FULL. That pack dropped zaden from the spine's own list because 'zaden is adjective-shaped with a full declension and stacks a new declining word directly on top of b2_neg_gen, taught one node earlier'. Both objections are gone at this distance: neg_gen is 70 nodes back and the adjective genitive is owned, so zaden costs one word rather than a system. THE ENGLISH TRAP GETS ITS OWN SLIDE and it is the reason this unit is worth building: English has FOUR ways of saying what Polish says with TWO. 'I'm not working yet' and 'I'm still not working' are both jeszcze nie pracuje; 'I don't work any more' and 'I no longer work' are both juz nie pracuje. An English speaker reaching for 'still' in a negative sentence will produce jeszcze and then stop, or reach for a word for 'longer' that does not exist. Taught as a four-into-two table, never derived. THE DOUBLE NEGATIVE IS RE-DRILLED AT ZERO COST, which is why this unit sits where it does: zaden takes the same obligatory second nie on the verb that nikt, nic, nigdy and nigdzie take, so slide 5 is b2_double_neg's rule seen a fifth time rather than a new claim. HOMOGRAPH AND CHUNK NOTES: problemu is TAUGHT only inside the frozen chunk nie ma problemu (= no problem), and Nie ma zadnego problemu is that chunk with a real slot opened in it - the dziekuje/ktorej/nowego chunk-to-slot treatment, said out loud on the slide. pomysl is TAUGHT but pomyslu is NOT, so the obvious English example 'no idea at all' was wanted and REFUSED rather than shipped on an untaught genitive. FENCED, all verified NEW: every oblique of zaden beyond the two genitives (zadnym, zadna-instrumental, zadnej-dative), the whole plural (zadne as a plural, zadnych, zadnym), and choc/jednak. zaden as a standalone pronoun (Zaden nie pracuje = none of them) is deliberately NOT taught and NEVER offered as a wrong choice, because it is correct Polish and marking it wrong would be the false-wrong James smoke-flagged on 2026-08-07. DISTRACTORS are agreement errors and word-order errors built from real taught forms - no fabricated non-words anywhere.

intro.title: Two words that turn into their own opposites
intro.body:
You have had już and jeszcze since the start of B2, both in their positive jobs: już is already or now, jeszcze is still.

Put a nie on the verb and neither of them simply becomes negative. Each one flips into a different idea altogether. już nie is not any more — something that used to be true and has stopped. jeszcze nie is not yet — something that is not true so far and is expected.

The pair is fixed in that order and the nie stays glued to the verb. There is no nie już.

intro.title: English has four ways of saying this. Polish has two.
intro.title_pl: cztery po angielsku, dwa po polsku
intro.body:
This is where an English speaker goes wrong, and it is worth reading the table in the English column first.

English splits each idea in two — not yet against still not, not any more against no longer — and none of those four phrases translates word for word. Polish does not split them at all. Two Polish sentences cover all four.

So the useful move is to stop looking for a word for still or for longer, and ask instead which of the two ideas you mean: has it stopped, or has it not started?

examples.en: The shop isn't open any more.

examples.pl: Mama jeszcze nie jest w domu.

intro.title: żaden — the negative word that agrees
intro.body:
B2 gave you four negative words that never change shape: nikt, nic, nigdy, nigdzie. żaden is the fifth and the last, and it is the only one that behaves like an adjective — it agrees with the noun it stands in front of.

It means not a single one, or not any. It cannot be used in a positive sentence at all; there is no sentence in Polish where żaden appears without a negation somewhere.

And, exactly like the other four, the verb still carries its own nie. Two negatives, as always.

intro.title: After a negated verb it takes the of-form, like every other object
intro.body:
B2 taught the rule and it has not changed: put a nie in front of a verb and its object moves into the of-form. Nie mam telefonu, not telefon.

żaden is an adjective, so it takes the adjective's of-form — the same -ego and -ej you already produce on dobrego, dobrej, nowego, nowej. Nothing new is being asked of you here; the ending is one you own and the noun behind it moves exactly as it did before.

Nie ma problemu is worth a second look. You have said it since B1 as one frozen piece meaning no problem. It turns out to have a slot in it, and this is the word that goes there.

examples.en: Mum hasn't got a phone at all.
My sister hasn't got a book at all.

intro.title: The five negative words, and the nie that never leaves
intro.body:
The set is closed now. These five are all of them, and every one of them takes a second nie on the verb — the rule you met at B2, seen for the last time.

Four of the five never change. żaden is the exception, and it changes for the reason an adjective changes: it has a noun to agree with.

English will not help you here. English allows only one negative per sentence and Polish demands two, so the sentence that sounds wrong in English is the correct one in Polish.

examples.en: The children aren't at school yet.
examples.pl: Dzieci jeszcze nie są w szkole.

quiz.prompt: You used to work, and now you don't →
quiz.explain: już nie is the pair for something that has stopped. jeszcze nie would say the opposite — that it has not started yet.

quiz.prompt: You start on Monday, so you haven't started →
quiz.explain: jeszcze nie covers both of English's ways of saying this — not working yet, and still not working.

quiz.prompt: The shop was open this morning and is closed now →
quiz.explain: It has stopped being true, so już nie. jeszcze nie would mean it has not opened yet — the other end of the day.

quiz.prompt: Mum is on her way and hasn't arrived →
choices: Mama jeszcze nie jest w domu.
Mama już nie jest w domu.
quiz.answer: Mama jeszcze nie jest w domu.
quiz.explain: Not there so far, and expected — that is jeszcze nie.

quiz.prompt: Not a single one — sklep is masculine →
quiz.explain: żaden agrees with its noun exactly as an adjective does, so a masculine noun takes żaden.

quiz.prompt: Not a single one — apteka is feminine →
quiz.explain: Feminine noun, feminine form — żadna, the same -a you have on dobra and nowa.

quiz.prompt: Not a single one — biuro is neuter →
You haven't got one at all — a phone →
quiz.explain: The nie on mam moves the object into the of-form, and żaden goes with it: żadnego telefonu, both words.

quiz.prompt: You haven't got one at all — a book →
quiz.explain: Feminine, and after the negation: żadnej książki. The -ej is the same ending you produce on dobrej and nowej.

quiz.prompt: You haven't got any at all — time →
quiz.explain: czas is masculine, so żadnego, and the negation puts the noun into czasu — the pair you have had since B2 with one word added in front.

quiz.prompt: There isn't one at all — a problem →
quiz.explain: Nie ma problemu was one frozen piece meaning no problem. This is the same sentence with a slot opened in it.
The second nie on the verb is obligatory, exactly as it is with żaden. nigdy nie pracuje is correct Polish too — it just says never rather than nobody.
